author: David Nott
text: Abstract In statistical modeling selecting the most appropriate model is crucial for accurate predictions and insightful interpretations This paper introduces a novel approach to model selection based on Coefficient Sign Prediction CSP methods which focus on estimating the expected signs of model coefficients rather than their magnitudes We propose a framework that integrates CSP methodologies into traditional model selection criteria enhancing the interpretability and robustness of the selected models The performance of the proposed methods is rigorously evaluated through simulation studies and realworld datasets highlighting their efficacy in capturing underlying relationships while reducing the complexity associated with coefficient estimation We demonstrate that models chosen via CSP methods not only align with theoretical expectations but also provide improved predictive performance over conventional selection methods This work contributes to the growing field of statistical model selection by offering a new perspective on coefficient relevance and providing practitioners with robust tools for model evaluation

author: David Nott
text: We consider a Bayesian model selection strategy based on predicting the signs of the coefficients in a regression model ie we consider identification of coefficients in a full or encompassing model for which we can confidently predict whether they are positive or negative This is useful when our main purpose in doing model selection is interpretation since the sign of a coefficient is often of primary importance for this task In the case of a linear model with standard noninformative prior we connect our sign coefficient prediction approach to the classical ZhengLoh procedure for model selection One advantage of our approach is that only specification of a prior on the full model is required unlike standard Bayesian variable selection approaches which require specification of prior distributions on parameters in all submodels and specification of a prior on the model itself We consider applying our method with proper hierarchical shrinkage priors which makes the procedure more useful in large p small n regression problems with more predictors than observations and in problems involving multicollinearity In these problems we may wish to do prediction by using shrinkage methods in the full model but interpreting which variables are important is also of interest We compare selection by using our coefficient sign prediction approach with the recently proposed elastic net procedure of Zou and Hastie and observe that our method shares some of the features of the elastic net such as a group selection property The method can be extended to more complex model selection problems such as selection on variance components in randomeffects models For selection on variance components where the parameter of interest is nonnegative and hence prediction of the sign of the parameter not the appropriate way to proceed we consider instead prediction of the sign of the score component for the parameter at zero obtaining a method that is related to classical score tests on variance components

author: David Nott
text: The use of the bootstrap test lends both elegance and simplicity to the analysis of complicated statistical problems Such a numerical approach yields an estimated Pvalue as a binomial proportion The purpose of this article is to recommend that confidence intervals for the bootstrap Pvalue be calculated routinely In constructing these intervals due consideration needs to be given to the Pvalues that may be close to or equal to zero We consider three instructive examples and related methods for designing the bootstrap sample size

author: David Nott
text: The forecasting skill of meteorologists is determined largely by their ability to interpret output from deterministic numerical weather prediction NWP models in the Light of local conditions Biases in the deterministic model may arise for many reasons including the inability to account for physical processes at a scale smaller than the grid used in the numerical solution of the model equations A statistical method for correction and interpretation of NWP model output is the model output statistics technique MOS where regression analysis is used to relate observations and NWP model predictions We describe a Bayesian hierarchical approach to MOS that was motivated by the need to develop sensible statistical corrections for recently opened stations with a short historical data record The strength of the Bayesian hierarchical formulation is its ability to combine information from stations with short and long observational records in a sensible way Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are used for computation and our approach is illustrated by using daily maximum temperature data from a network of stations in the Sydney area

author: David Nott
text: Numerical weather prediction NWP models serve as the backbone of modern meteorology providing essential forecasts for weather and climate phenomena However the inherent complexity and deterministic nature of these models often lead to systematic biases and errors in their output particularly in local and shortterm forecasts This paper presents a statistical correction framework designed to enhance the accuracy of a widely used deterministic NWP model Leveraging a combination of historical observational data and model output we implement advanced statistical techniques including regression analysis machine learning algorithms and Bayesian approaches to identify and correct biases in the models predictions The framework is evaluated through comprehensive case studies and crossvalidation methods demonstrating significant improvements in forecast skill across various meteorological parameters including temperature precipitation and wind speed Our findings highlight the potential of statistical postprocessing to refine deterministic forecasts offering a pathway to more reliable weather predictions that can better serve the needs of meteorological services and the community at large The proposed methodology not only addresses the limitations of current NWP models but also opens avenues for future research in hybrid modeling approaches that integrate deterministic and statistical techniques

author: David Nott
text: Multivariate adaptive regression spline fitting or MARS Friedman provides a useful methodology for flexible adaptive regression with many predictors The MARS methodology produces an estimate of the mean response that is a linear combination of adaptively chosen basis functions Recently a Bayesian version of MARS has been proposed Denison Mallick and Smith a Holmes and Denison combining the MARS methodology with the benefits of Bayesian methods for accounting for model uncertainty to achieve improvements in predictive performance In implementation of the Bayesian MARS approach Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are used for computations in which at each iteration of the algorithm it is proposed to change the current model by either a Adding a basis function birth step b Deleting a basis function death step or c Altering an existing basis function change step In the algorithm of Denison Mallick and Smith a when a birth step is proposed the type of basis function is determined by simulation from the prior This works well in problems with a small number of predictors is simple to program and leads to a simple form for MetropolisHastings acceptance probabilities However in problems with very large numbers of predictors where many of the predictors are useless it may be difficult to find interesting interactions with such an approach In the original MARS algorithm of Friedman a heuristic is used of building up higher order interactions from lower order ones which greatly reduces the complexity of the search for good basis functions to add to the model While we do not exactly follow the intuition of the original MARS algorithm in this paper we nevertheless suggest a similar idea in which the MetropolisHastings proposals of Denison Mallick and Smith a are altered to allow dependence on the current model Our modification allows more rapid identification and exploration of important interactions especially in problems with very large numbers of predictor variables and many useless predictors Performance of the algorithms is compared in simulation studies

author: David Nott
text: Mixtures of linear mixed models MLMMs are useful for clustering grouped data and can be estimated by likelihood maximization through the Expectation Maximization algorithm A suitable number of components is then determined conventionally by comparing different mixture models using penalized loglikelihood criteria such as Bayesian information criterion We propose fitting MLMMs with variational methods which can perform parameter estimation and model selection simultaneously We describe a variational approximation for MLMMs where the variational lower bound is in closed form allowing for fast evaluation and develop a novel variational greedy algorithm for model selection and learning of the mixture components This approach handles algorithm initialization and returns a plausible number of mixture components automatically In cases of weak identifiability of certain model parameters we use hierarchical centering to reparameterize the model and show empirically that there is a gain in efficiency in variational algorithms similar to that in Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithms Related to this we prove that the approximate rate of convergence of variational algorithms by Gaussian approximation is equal to that of the corresponding Gibbs sampler which suggests that reparameterizations can lead to improved convergence in variational algorithms just as in MCMC algorithms Supplementary materials for the article are available online

author: David Nott
text: The Laplace approximation is a foundational technique for approximating integrals of the form e dx in statistical inference and Bayesian analysis This paper presents a generalization of the classical Laplace approximation extending its applicability to a broader class of functions and multidimensional integrals We introduce a refined methodology that accommodates more complex landscapes of the function fx including those with multiple local minima and saddle points Through a combination of perturbation techniques and higherorder Taylor expansions we derive an asymptotic expansion that quantifies the corrections to the standard Laplace approximation Additionally we showcase our generalized approach through several empirical examples demonstrating improvements in accuracy and convergence rates in practical applications particularly in highdimensional parameter spaces The proposed framework not only enhances the robustness of the Laplace method but also provides a pathway for future research on approximation techniques in statistics Our findings suggest that this generalization can significantly aid in developing more efficient algorithms for inference in complex Bayesian models

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we present a comprehensive analysis of the bootstrap pvalue methodology emphasizing the derivation of confidence intervals for bootstrap pvalues and the implications for sample size calculations in bootstrap hypothesis testing We begin by reviewing the conventional applications of bootstrap techniques in estimating pvalues and highlight the importance of quantifying uncertainty in these estimates through confidence intervals By developing novel statistical frameworks we establish methodologies for constructing confidence intervals for bootstrap pvalues that account for variability inherent in the resampling process We further explore the relationship between desired statistical power and required sample size in the context of bootstrap tests providing practical guidelines for researchers Our simulations demonstrate the robustness of our proposed methods across various distributions underscoring their utility in improving the reliability of bootstrap inference This work integrates theoretical insights with practical applications enhancing the understanding of bootstrap methods in statistical testing scenarios and offering valuable tools for researchers in diverse fields

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we introduce a novel variational approximation approach for estimating parameters in mixtures of linear mixed models MLMMs which are increasingly utilized to analyze complex hierarchical data structures characterized by diverse subpopulations Traditional methods for fitting MLMMs such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference often face challenges related to computational inefficiency and convergence difficulties particularly in highdimensional settings or when the number of mixture components is large Our proposed variational framework leverages the principles of variational inference to provide an efficient and scalable solution We develop a set of variational families tailored for the mixture components and derive a lower bound on the marginal likelihood which we maximize to obtain approximate posterior distributions Through extensive simulation studies and realworld applications we demonstrate that our approach not only achieves competitive performance in terms of parameter estimation and model selection but also significantly reduces computational time compared to traditional methods We further illustrate the versatility of our method by applying it to a variety of datasets highlighting its effectiveness in uncovering latent structures and providing insights into the underlying population heterogeneity This work contributes to the field of statistical modeling by offering a robust framework for addressing the complexities associated with MLMMs paving the way for future research in variational methods for mixture models

author: David Nott
text: Hierarchical and empirical Bayes approaches to inference are attractive for data arising from microarray gene expression studies because of their ability to borrow strength across genes in making inferences Here we focus on the simplest case where we have data from replicated two colour arrays which compare two samples and where we wish to decide which genes are differentially expressed and obtain estimates of operating characteristics such as false discovery rates The purpose of this paper is to examine the frequentist performance of Bayesian variable selection approaches to this problem for different prior specifications and to examine the effect on inference of commonly used empirical Bayes approximations to hierarchical Bayes procedures The paper makes three main contributions First we describe how the log odds of differential expression can usually be computed analytically in the case where a double tailed exponential prior is used for gene effects rather than a normal prior which gives an alternative to the commonly used Bstatistic for ranking genes in simple comparative experiments The second contribution of the paper is to compare empirical Bayes procedures for detecting differential expression with hierarchical Bayes methods which account for uncertainty in prior hyperparameters to examine how much is lost in using the commonly employed empirical Bayes approximations Third we describe an efficient MCMC scheme for carrying out the computations required for the hierarchical Bayes procedures Comparisons are made via simulation studies where the simulated data are obtained by fitting models to some real microarray data sets The results have implications for analysis of microarray data using parametric hierarchical and empirical Bayes methods for more complex experimental designs generally we find that the empirical Bayes methods work well which supports their use in the analysis of more complex experiments when a full hierarchical Bayes analysis would impose heavy computational demands c Elsevier Inc

author: David Nott
text: AbstractMicroarray experiments have revolutionized genomics by enabling the simultaneous analysis of thousands of genes leading to insights into gene expression patterns associated with various biological conditions However the high dimensionality of microarray data poses significant challenges for variable selection necessitating robust statistical methodologies that can effectively discern informative predictors from noise In this paper we propose a Hierarchical Bayes framework for variable selection that accommodates the unique characteristics of microarray data particularly the presence of correlated predictors and sparsity in signal Our approach integrates hierarchical modeling with Bayesian variable selection to provide a flexible and principled mechanism for identifying genes relevant to specific phenotypes We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through extensive simulation studies and apply it to realworld microarray datasets revealing notable improvements in prediction accuracy and interpretability compared to traditional variable selection techniques The implications of our findings extend to enhanced understanding of gene interactions and the development of targeted diagnostics in personalized medicine

author: David Nott
text: AbstractIn the context of Bayesian modeling particularly when applied to Mars exploration data the challenge of efficiently estimating parameters in models with a large number of predictors is paramount This paper presents novel sampling schemes designed to enhance the efficiency of posterior sampling in Bayesian models characterized by highdimensional predictor spaces Building on the foundations of Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods we introduce a hybrid sampling strategy that incorporates variancereduction techniques and adaptive proposals tailored specifically for the complexities inherent in Mars datasets which often exhibit multicollinearity and nonlinear relationships among predictors We conduct extensive simulations to compare our approach against traditional MCMC methods focusing on convergence rates effective sample sizes and computational costs Results indicate significant improvements in sampling efficiency and parameter estimation accuracy demonstrating the applicability of our schemes to largescale Bayesian inference problems Our findings not only contribute to the advancement of statistical methodologies for planetary science but also provide a framework for future research in highdimensional Bayesian modeling across various domains Key words Bayesian modeling Mars exploration posterior sampling Markov Chain Monte Carlo highdimensional inference variance reduction

author: David Nott
text: Laplace approximation is one commonly used approach to the calculation of difficult integrals arising in Bayesian inference and the analysis of random effects models Here we outline a procedure which is an extension of the Laplace approximation and which attempts to find changes of variable for which the integrand becomes approximately a product of onedimensional functions When the integrand is a product of onedimensional functions an approximation to the integral can be obtained using onediniensional quadrature The approximation is exact for a broader class of functions than the ordinary Laplace approximation and can be applied when the integrand is not smooth at lie mode As an illustration of this last point we consider Calculation of marginal likelihoods for smoothing parameter selection in the lasso C Elsevier BV

author: David Nott
text: We propose the Bayesian adaptive Lasso BaLasso for variable selection and coefficient estimation in linear regression The BaLasso is adaptive to the signal level by adopting different shrinkage for different coefficients Furthermore we provide a model selection machinery for the BaLasso by assessing the posterior conditional mode estimates motivated by the hierarchical Bayesian interpretation of the Lasso Our formulation also permits prediction using a model averaging strategy We discuss other variants of this new approach and provide a unified framework for variable selection using flexible penalties Empirical evidence of the attractiveness of the method is demonstrated via extensive simulation studies and data analysis

author: David Nott
text: We propose a shrinkage procedure for simultaneous variable selection and estimation in generalized linear models GLMs with an explicit predictive motivation The procedure estimates the coefficients by minimizing the KullbackLeibler divergence of a set of predictive distributions to the corresponding predictive distributions for the full model subject to an l constraint on the coefficient vector This results in selection of a parsimonious model with similar predictive performance to the full model Thanks to its similar form to the original Lasso problem for GLMs our procedure can benefit from available l regularization path algorithms Simulation studies and real data examples confirm the efficiency of our method in terms of predictive performance on future observations

author: David Nott
text: The effects of different parametrizations on the convergence of Bayesian computational algorithms for hierarchical models are well explored Techniques such as centering noncentering and partial noncentering can be used to accelerate convergence in MCMC and EM algorithms but are still not well studied for variational Bayes VB methods As a fast deterministic approach to posterior approximation VB is attracting increasing interest due to its suitability for large highdimensional data Use of different parametrizations for VB has not only computational but also statistical implications as different parametrizations are associated with different factorized posterior approximations We examine the use of partially noncentered parametrizations in VB for generalized linear mixed models GLMMs Our paper makes four contributions First we show how to implement an algorithm called nonconjugate variational message passing for GLMMs Second we show that the partially noncentered parametrization can adapt to the quantity of information in the data and determine a parametrization close to optimal Third we show that partial noncentering can accelerate convergence and produce more accurate posterior approximations than centering or noncentering Finally we demonstrate how the variational lower bound produced as part of the computation can be useful for model selection

author: David Nott
text: Our article presents a general treatment of the linear regression model in which the error distribution is modelled nonparametrically and the error variances may be heteroscedastic thus eliminating the need to transform the dependent variable in many data sets The mean and variance components of the model may be either parametric or nonparametric with parsimony achieved through variable selection and model averaging A Bayesian approach is used for inference with priors that are databased so that estimation can be carried out automatically with minimal input by the user A Dirichlet process mixture prior is used to model the error distribution nonparametrically when there are no regressors in the model the method reduces to Bayesian density estimation and we show that in this case the estimator compares favourably with a wellregarded plugin density estimator We also consider a method for checking the fit of the full model The methodology is applied to a number of simulated and real examples and is shown to work well

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we introduce a novel variational approximation approach for estimating parameters in mixtures of linear mixed models MLMMs which are increasingly utilized to analyze complex hierarchical data structures characterized by diverse subpopulations Traditional methods for fitting MLMMs such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference often face challenges related to computational inefficiency and convergence difficulties particularly in highdimensional settings or when the number of mixture components is large Our proposed variational framework leverages the principles of variational inference to provide an efficient and scalable solution We develop a set of variational families tailored for the mixture components and derive a lower bound on the marginal likelihood which we maximize to obtain approximate posterior distributions Through extensive simulation studies and realworld applications we demonstrate that our approach not only achieves competitive performance in terms of parameter estimation and model selection but also significantly reduces computational time compared to traditional methods We further illustrate the versatility of our method by applying it to a variety of datasets highlighting its effectiveness in uncovering latent structures and providing insights into the underlying population heterogeneity This work contributes to the field of statistical modeling by offering a robust framework for addressing the complexities associated with MLMMs paving the way for future research in variational methods for mixture models

author: David Nott
text: Dirichlet Process Mixture Models DPMMs are powerful tools for nonparametric clustering allowing for flexible modeling of data with an unknown number of clusters However traditional fitting methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC approaches often suffer from computational inefficiencies particularly in large datasets In this paper we propose a novel sequential algorithm that significantly enhances the speed and efficiency of fitting DPMMs Our method leverages sequential data processing and an adaptive sampling strategy to incrementally update cluster assignments and parameters facilitating realtime inference We provide a theoretical foundation for our algorithm proving its consistency and convergence properties Through extensive simulations and realworld applications we demonstrate that our sequential approach outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed and accuracy achieving comparable or superior clustering results in significantly shorter computational time This work highlights the potential of sequential algorithms in advancing the practical use of DPMMs and opens avenues for further exploration in nonparametric statistical methods

author: David Nott
text: In statistical modeling the assumption of constant variance or homoscedasticity in linear regression is often violated leading to inefficient estimates and invalid inference This paper presents a general approach to heteroscedastic linear regression that addresses this critical limitation We propose a framework that combines robust statistical techniques with flexible modeling of variance structures allowing for adaptive adjustments to error variances across different levels of predictor variables Our methodology employs generalized least squares GLS and quantified maximum likelihood estimation integrating diagnostics for identifying and testing heteroscedasticity We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through simulation studies and realworld applications demonstrating significant improvements in parameter estimation and hypothesis testing compared to traditional ordinary least squares OLS methods Our findings provide practitioners with a robust toolkit for handling heteroscedasticity in linear regression analysis contributing to more reliable and accurate predictive modeling across various fields of research

author: David Nott
text: Generalized linear mixed models GLMMs are widely used for analyzing correlated data with nonnormal response distributions Traditional inference methods such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian approaches using full parametrizations can be computationally intensive and sensitive to model specifications particularly in highdimensional settings In this paper we introduce a variational inference framework for GLMMs that employs partially noncentered parametrizations This approach strikes a balance between alleviating the computational burden of traditional methods and enhancing robustness to prior choices We derive the variational lower bound facilitating efficient optimization using stochastic gradient descent techniques Through extensive simulation studies and real data applications we demonstrate that our method yields accurate parameter estimates and credible intervals while significantly reducing computational time compared to Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods The proposed variational approach not only provides a scalable solution for large datasets and complex models but also opens new avenues for the application of GLMMs in fields such as biostatistics ecology and social sciences Our findings underscore the efficacy of using partially noncentered parametrizations in variational inference for mixed models positioning this methodology as a valuable tool for statisticians and data scientists alike

author: David Nott
text: AbstractIn this paper we introduce the Bayesian Adaptive Lasso a novel framework that combines the strengths of Bayesian inference with the adaptive Lasso regression technique for variable selection and regularization The Adaptive Lasso is known for its ability to perform variable selection while maintaining oracle properties yet it relies heavily on the choice of penalty and tuning parameters Our proposed Bayesian approach mitigates this issue by employing a hierarchical prior structure that allows for automatic tuning of the regularization parameters resulting in enhanced flexibility and adaptability to diverse datasetsWe derive the full posterior distribution and present an efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithm for sampling from it enabling practitioners to make robust inferences in highdimensional settings Extensive simulations illustrate the improved variable selection performance and estimation accuracy of our method compared to traditional Lasso and frequentist adaptive Lasso methods Furthermore we apply our Bayesian Adaptive Lasso to realworld datasets across various domains demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying significant predictors while controlling for overfitting This work advances the methodology of highdimensional Bayesian regression and opens new pathways for incorporating prior information into variable selection processes

author: David Nott
text: AbstractIn the realm of predictive modeling the Lasso Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator has emerged as a powerful tool for variable selection and regularization This paper introduces an enhanced framework termed The Predictive Lasso which expands upon traditional Lasso techniques by integrating a robust predictive validation approach We investigate the performance of the Predictive Lasso in highdimensional settings where the number of predictors significantly exceeds the number of observations Through a series of simulation studies and realdata applications we demonstrate that our method not only maintains variable selection integrity but also improves predictive accuracy compared to standard Lasso implementations Additionally we explore the theoretical underpinnings of the Predictive Lasso offering guarantees on estimation consistency and predictive performance Our findings suggest that the Predictive Lasso is a compelling alternative for statisticians and data scientists seeking to optimize model predictive power while addressing the challenges posed by multicollinearity and overfitting inherent in modern datasets The results highlight the importance of balancing model complexity with predictive reliability paving the way for future research in the domain of regularized regression techniques

author: David Nott
text: In this article we propose an improvement on the sequential updating and greedy search SUGS algorithm for fast fitting of Dirichlet process mixture models The SUGS algorithm provides a means for very fast approximate Bayesian inference for mixture data which is particularly of use when datasets are so large that many standard Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithms cannot be applied efficiently or take a prohibitively long time to converge In particular these ideas are used to initially interrogate the data and to refine models such that one can potentially apply exact data analysis later on SUGS relies upon sequentially allocating data to clusters and proceeding with an update of the posterior on the subsequent allocations and parameters which assumes this allocation is correct Our modification softens this approach by providing a probability distribution over allocations with a similar computational cost this approach has an interpretation as a variational Bayes procedure and hence we term it variational SUGS VSUGS It is shown in simulated examples that VSUGS can outperform in terms of density estimation and classification a version of the SUGS algorithm in many scenarios In addition we present a data analysis for flow cytometry data and SNP data via a threeclass Dirichlet process mixture model illustrating the apparent improvement over the original SUGS algorithm

text: We consider parameter estimation for certain random set models for image data For the spatial models considered here a full likelihoodbased approach to this problem is often difficult since the likelihood generally cannot be computed for images of typical size This has motivated the consideration of various less computationally demanding parameter estimation techniques We discuss one method based on likelihoods for small subsets of the data Consideration of the basic technique within the framework of the theory of estimating functions leads to a weighted version ofthe basic approach Results of a simulation study are reported for some variants of the Boolean model and excursion sets of random fields The methods are illustrated for some data on the spatial incidence of heather

author: David Nott
text: Our paper proposes adaptive Monte Carlo sampling schemes for Bayesian variable selection in linear regression that improve on standard Markov chain methods We do so by considering MetropolisHastings proposals that make use of accumulated information about the posterior distribution obtained during sampling Adaptation needs to be done carefully to ensure that sampling is from the correct ergodic distribution We give conditions for the validity of an adaptive sampling scheme in this problem and for simulating from a distribution on a finite state space in general and suggest a class of adaptive proposal densities which uses best linear prediction to approximate the Gibbs sampler Our sampling scheme is computationally much faster per iteration than the Gibbs sampler and when this is taken into account the efficiency gains when using our sampling scheme compared to alternative approaches are substantial in terms of precision of estimation of posterior quantities of interest for a given amount of computation time We compare our method with other sampling schemes for examples involving both real and simulated data The methodology developed in the paper can be extended to variable selection in more general problems

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we propose a novel pairwise likelihood approach for statistical inference in image models addressing the challenges posed by highdimensional data and complex dependencies among pixel values Traditional likelihood methods often struggle with the intricacies of image structures leading to computational intractability and inefficiencies Our pairwise likelihood framework simplifies inference by focusing on relationships between pairs of pixels allowing for effective handling of dependencies while significantly reducing computational burden We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through simulations and real image datasets comparing it with established full likelihood and pseudolikelihood techniques Our results highlight the advantages of pairwise likelihood in terms of parameter estimation accuracy and computational efficiency particularly in largescale image analysis scenarios Finally we discuss potential applications in various fields including computer vision medical imaging and remote sensing illustrating the versatility and robustness of our approach for extracting meaningful insights from complex image data

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we present a novel stochastic variational framework for fitting and diagnosing Generalized Linear Mixed Models GLMMs which are widely used for analyzing correlated data and handling complex random effects structures Traditional fitting methods such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference often face challenges relating to computational efficiency and model complexity especially as the dimensionality of the random effects increases Our proposed framework leverages variational inference techniques to approximate posterior distributions effectively providing a computationally tractable approach that scales with highdimensional data We develop a flexible stochastic variational algorithm that incorporates automatic differentiation and parallelization ensuring robust and efficient estimation of the model parameters Additionally we introduce diagnostic tools within this framework that allow practitioners to assess model fit and identify potential misspecifications enhancing the interpretability of the results We validate our approach through extensive simulations and apply it to realworld datasets demonstrating its superiority over traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and computational speed Our contributions pave the way for more accessible and efficient analysis of GLMMs in diverse applications across various fields

text: In the realm of Bayesian statistics variable selection plays a crucial role in model building and interpretation Traditional approaches often face challenges related to computational efficiency and the ability to adaptively identify relevant predictors particularly in highdimensional settings This paper introduces an innovative adaptive sampling strategy tailored for Bayesian variable selection enhancing both estimations of posterior probabilities and computational feasibility By leveraging adaptive Monte Carlo techniques and dynamic Bayesian updating our method selectively samples variables based on their contributions to model fit allowing for realtime adjustments as new data becomes available We benchmark our approach against existing methodologies using both simulated and real datasets demonstrating significant improvements in variable selection accuracy and reduced computational time Our findings suggest that adaptive sampling not only optimizes the selection process but also provides a robust framework for handling uncertainty in variable inclusion The proposed method offers a promising avenue for researchers seeking efficient and effective Bayesian variable selection techniques in complex modeling scenarios

author: David Nott
text: In stochastic variational inference the variational Bayes objective function is optimized using stochastic gradient approximation where gradients computed on small random subsets of data are used to approximate the true gradient over the whole data set This enables complex models to be fit to large data sets as data can be processed in minibatches In this article we extend stochastic variational inference for conjugateexponential models to nonconjugate models and present a stochastic nonconjugate variational message passing algorithm for fitting generalized linear mixed models that is scalable to large data sets In addition we show that diagnostics for priorlikelihood conflict which are useful for Bayesian model criticism can be obtained from nonconjugate variational message passing automatically as an alternative to simulationbased Markov chain Monte Carlo methods Finally we demonstrate that for moderatesized data sets convergence can be accelerated by using the stochastic version of nonconjugate variational message passing in the initial stage of optimization before switching to the standard version

author: David Nott
text: Generalized linear mixed models GLMMs are widely used for analyzing correlated data with nonnormal response distributions Traditional inference methods such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian approaches using full parametrizations can be computationally intensive and sensitive to model specifications particularly in highdimensional settings In this paper we introduce a variational inference framework for GLMMs that employs partially noncentered parametrizations This approach strikes a balance between alleviating the computational burden of traditional methods and enhancing robustness to prior choices We derive the variational lower bound facilitating efficient optimization using stochastic gradient descent techniques Through extensive simulation studies and real data applications we demonstrate that our method yields accurate parameter estimates and credible intervals while significantly reducing computational time compared to Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods The proposed variational approach not only provides a scalable solution for large datasets and complex models but also opens new avenues for the application of GLMMs in fields such as biostatistics ecology and social sciences Our findings underscore the efficacy of using partially noncentered parametrizations in variational inference for mixed models positioning this methodology as a valuable tool for statisticians and data scientists alike

author: David Nott
text: AbstractIn the realm of predictive modeling the Lasso Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator has emerged as a powerful tool for variable selection and regularization This paper introduces an enhanced framework termed The Predictive Lasso which expands upon traditional Lasso techniques by integrating a robust predictive validation approach We investigate the performance of the Predictive Lasso in highdimensional settings where the number of predictors significantly exceeds the number of observations Through a series of simulation studies and realdata applications we demonstrate that our method not only maintains variable selection integrity but also improves predictive accuracy compared to standard Lasso implementations Additionally we explore the theoretical underpinnings of the Predictive Lasso offering guarantees on estimation consistency and predictive performance Our findings suggest that the Predictive Lasso is a compelling alternative for statisticians and data scientists seeking to optimize model predictive power while addressing the challenges posed by multicollinearity and overfitting inherent in modern datasets The results highlight the importance of balancing model complexity with predictive reliability paving the way for future research in the domain of regularized regression techniques

author: David Nott
text: AbstractIn the context of Bayesian modeling particularly when applied to Mars exploration data the challenge of efficiently estimating parameters in models with a large number of predictors is paramount This paper presents novel sampling schemes designed to enhance the efficiency of posterior sampling in Bayesian models characterized by highdimensional predictor spaces Building on the foundations of Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods we introduce a hybrid sampling strategy that incorporates variancereduction techniques and adaptive proposals tailored specifically for the complexities inherent in Mars datasets which often exhibit multicollinearity and nonlinear relationships among predictors We conduct extensive simulations to compare our approach against traditional MCMC methods focusing on convergence rates effective sample sizes and computational costs Results indicate significant improvements in sampling efficiency and parameter estimation accuracy demonstrating the applicability of our schemes to largescale Bayesian inference problems Our findings not only contribute to the advancement of statistical methodologies for planetary science but also provide a framework for future research in highdimensional Bayesian modeling across various domains Key words Bayesian modeling Mars exploration posterior sampling Markov Chain Monte Carlo highdimensional inference variance reduction

author: David Nott
text: We propose a shrinkage procedure for simultaneous variable selection and estimation in generalized linear models GLMs with an explicit predictive motivation The procedure estimates the coefficients by minimizing the KullbackLeibler divergence of a set of predictive distributions to the corresponding predictive distributions for the full model subject to an l constraint on the coefficient vector This results in selection of a parsimonious model with similar predictive performance to the full model Thanks to its similar form to the original Lasso problem for GLMs our procedure can benefit from available l regularization path algorithms Simulation studies and real data examples confirm the efficiency of our method in terms of predictive performance on future observations

author: David Nott
text: Understanding wind patterns in complex environments such as Sydney Harbour is crucial for various applications including urban planning maritime safety and environmental monitoring In this study we develop a comprehensive spacetime statistical model to analyze wind speed and direction in the Sydney Harbour region leveraging a series of highresolution meteorological data collected over several years Our approach incorporates spatiotemporal dependencies by utilizing Gaussian processes allowing us to capture localized variations and nonstationarity inherent in wind behavior influenced by geographical features and urban development We employ a Bayesian framework for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification facilitating robust predictions and insights into the dynamic wind patterns over time The models performance is evaluated against traditional temporal models demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and reliability for both shortterm forecasting and longterm trend analysis The results provide valuable guidance for stakeholders in Sydney offering a clearer understanding of wind dynamics that can inform decisionmaking processes in diverse sectors This work contributes to the growing field of environmental statistics and emphasizes the necessity of incorporating spatial and temporal dimensions in modeling atmospheric phenomena

author: David Nott
text: This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the mean and variance functions in regression models through a locally adaptive semiparametric framework We propose a generalized method that combines nonparametric techniques with parametric structures to estimate both the expected response and the associated variability allowing for flexibility in capturing complex relationships in the data Our approach utilizes local polynomial fitting to ensure the estimation remains responsive to local data patterns while being grounded in a coherent semiparametric model We rigorously derive the asymptotic properties of the estimators demonstrating their consistency and efficiency in a variety of scenarios Simulation studies illustrate the advantages of our method over traditional parametric and nonparametric techniques particularly in the presence of heteroscedasticity and nonlinear relationships The practical applicability of our approach is further validated through an analysis of realworld datasets highlighting its effectiveness in capturing intricate regression dynamics Our findings underscore the importance of locally adaptive strategies in enhancing the accuracy of mean and variance function estimation in regression contexts

author: David Nott
text: This paper develops a space time statistical model for local forecasting of surface level wind fields in a coastal region with complex topography The statistical model makes use of output from deterministic numerical weather prediction models which are able to produce forecasts of surface wind fields on a spatial grid When predicting surface winds at observing stations errors can arise due to sub grid scale processes not adequately captured by the numerical weather prediction model and the statistical model attempts to correct for these influences In particular it uses information from observing stations within the study region as well as topographic information to account for local bias Bayesian methods for inference are used in the model with computations carried out using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms Empirical performance of the model is described illustrating that a structured Bayesian approach to complicated space time models of the type considered in this paper can be readily implemented and can lead to improvements in forecasting over traditional methods

author: David Nott
text: This article proposes a Bayesian method for estimating a heteroscedastic regression model with Gaussian errors where the mean and the log variance are modeled as linear combinations of explanatory variables We use Bayesian variable selection priors and model averaging to make the estimation more efficient The model is made semiparametric by allowing explanatory variables to enter the mean and log variance flexibly by representing a covariate effect as a linear combination of basis functions Our methodology for estimating flexible effects is locally adaptive in the sense that it works well when the flexible effects vary rapidly in some parts of the predictor space but only slowly in other parts Our article develops an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation method to sample from the posterior distribution and applies the methodology to a number of simulated and real examples

author: David Nott
text: The use of the bootstrap test lends both elegance and simplicity to the analysis of complicated statistical problems Such a numerical approach yields an estimated Pvalue as a binomial proportion The purpose of this article is to recommend that confidence intervals for the bootstrap Pvalue be calculated routinely In constructing these intervals due consideration needs to be given to the Pvalues that may be close to or equal to zero We consider three instructive examples and related methods for designing the bootstrap sample size

author: David Nott
text: This paper introduces a novel model selection approach for nonparametric regression based on a signbased loss criterion Traditional model selection techniques often rely on criteria such as Akaike Information Criterion AIC or Bayesian Information Criterion BIC which can be sensitive to outliers and may not adequately capture the underlying structure of the data We propose a signbased loss function that emphasizes the preservation of monotonic trends and directional relationships present in the regression data aiming to enhance predictive accuracy and interpretability Our framework involves a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the signbased loss showcasing its consistency and robustness compared to conventional loss functions We perform extensive simulations to compare our method against standard model selection criteria across various nonparametric regression settings The results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior model selection performance particularly in scenarios with high noise levels and complex data structures Additionally we apply our method to realworld datasets to illustrate its practical utility and effectiveness in improving predictive modeling The findings suggest that incorporating signbased considerations in model selection can lead to more reliable and insightful nonparametric regression outcomes This work lays the groundwork for further exploration of loss functions in statistical modeling emphasizing the importance of directional information in complex data analysis

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we propose a novel approach to regression density estimation that integrates variational methods with stochastic approximation techniques Traditional regression methods often struggle with capturing complex relationships within highdimensional data particularly when seeking to estimate the underlying density of responses Our method leverages the strengths of variational inference to provide a flexible probabilistic framework for modeling these complex relationships while simultaneously addressing the computational challenges often encountered in highdimensional settings We introduce a variational regression density estimation framework that allows for the incorporation of prior information and uncertainty quantification This framework is further enhanced by employing stochastic approximation techniques which facilitate efficient optimization in the presence of large datasets and highdimensional feature spaces Our theoretical analysis demonstrates the convergence properties of the proposed algorithms while empirical results on simulated and realworld datasets illustrate the effectiveness of our method compared to existing density estimation approaches The results show that our approach not only yields accurate and reliable density estimates but also provides insights into the underlying structure of the data This work bridges the gap between variational methods and stochastic optimization contributing a valuable tool for practitioners in regression analysis and density estimation tasks We discuss potential applications and future research directions emphasizing the importance of combining robust statistical methodologies with modern computational strategies

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we present a novel stochastic variational framework for fitting and diagnosing Generalized Linear Mixed Models GLMMs which are widely used for analyzing correlated data and handling complex random effects structures Traditional fitting methods such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference often face challenges relating to computational efficiency and model complexity especially as the dimensionality of the random effects increases Our proposed framework leverages variational inference techniques to approximate posterior distributions effectively providing a computationally tractable approach that scales with highdimensional data We develop a flexible stochastic variational algorithm that incorporates automatic differentiation and parallelization ensuring robust and efficient estimation of the model parameters Additionally we introduce diagnostic tools within this framework that allow practitioners to assess model fit and identify potential misspecifications enhancing the interpretability of the results We validate our approach through extensive simulations and apply it to realworld datasets demonstrating its superiority over traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and computational speed Our contributions pave the way for more accessible and efficient analysis of GLMMs in diverse applications across various fields

author: David Nott
text: In this paper we present a comprehensive analysis of the bootstrap pvalue methodology emphasizing the derivation of confidence intervals for bootstrap pvalues and the implications for sample size calculations in bootstrap hypothesis testing We begin by reviewing the conventional applications of bootstrap techniques in estimating pvalues and highlight the importance of quantifying uncertainty in these estimates through confidence intervals By developing novel statistical frameworks we establish methodologies for constructing confidence intervals for bootstrap pvalues that account for variability inherent in the resampling process We further explore the relationship between desired statistical power and required sample size in the context of bootstrap tests providing practical guidelines for researchers Our simulations demonstrate the robustness of our proposed methods across various distributions underscoring their utility in improving the reliability of bootstrap inference This work integrates theoretical insights with practical applications enhancing the understanding of bootstrap methods in statistical testing scenarios and offering valuable tools for researchers in diverse fields

author: David Nott
text: In parametric regression models the sign of a coefficient often plays an important role in its interpretation One possible approach to model selection in these situations is to consider a loss function that formulates prediction of the sign of a coefficient as a decision problem Taking a Bayesian approach we extend this idea of a sign based loss for selection to more complex situations In generalized additive models we consider prediction of the sign of the derivative of an additive term at a set of predictors Being able to predict the sign of the derivative at some point that is whether a term is increasing or decreasing is one approach to selection of terms in additive modelling when interpretation is the main goal For models with interactions prediction of the sign of a higher order derivative can be used similarly There are many advantages to our signbased strategy for selection one can work in a full or encompassing model without the need to specify priors on a model space and without needing to specify priors on parameters in submodels Also avoiding a search over a large model space can simplify computation We consider shrinkage prior specifications on smoothing parameters that allow for good predictive performance in models with large numbers of terms without the need for selection and a frequentist calibration of the parameter in our signbased loss function when it is desired to control a false selection rate for interpretation

author: David Nott
text: Regression density estimation is the problem of flexibly estimating a response distribution as a function of covariates An important approach to regression density estimation uses finite mixture models and our article considers flexible mixtures of heteroscedastic regression MHR models where the response distribution is a normal mixture with the component means variances and mixture weights all varying as a function of covariates Our article develops fast variational approximation VA methods for inference Our motivation is that alternative computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods for fitting mixture models are difficult to apply when it is desired to fit models repeatedly in exploratory analysis and model choice Our article makes three contributions First a VA for MHR models is described where the variational lower bound is in closed form Second the basic approximation can be improved by using stochastic approximation SA methods to perturb the initial solution to attain higher accuracy Third the advantages of our approach for model choice and evaluation compared with MCMCbased approaches are illustrated These advantages are particularly compelling for time series data where repeated refitting for onestepahead prediction in model choice and diagnostics and in rollingwindow computations is very common Supplementary materials for the article are available online

author: David Nott
text: This paper explores the relationship between the Ensemble Kalman Filter EnKF and Approximate Bayesian Computation ABC frameworks demonstrating that the EnKF can be viewed as a specialized ABC algorithm for statistical inference in nonlinear dynamical systems We first provide a comprehensive overview of the EnKF highlighting its role in state estimation and uncertainty quantification within the context of Bayesian filtering Then we develop a theoretical foundation that connects the two methodologies showing how the EnKF operates under the principles of ABC by approximating posterior distributions through an ensemble of particle states We illustrate this connection through a series of simulations and theoretical examples revealing that the ensemble samples generated by the EnKF correspond to the accepted proposals in an ABC setting Furthermore we discuss the implications of this perspective for enhancing the interpretability of the EnKF as well as for improving its performance in highdimensional parameter spaces Our findings suggest that integrating concepts from ABC into the EnKF framework could lead to innovative approaches for tackling challenges in data assimilation and model calibration Ultimately this work contributes to a deeper understanding of both the EnKF and ABC opening avenues for future research at the intersection of Bayesian statistics and numerical filtering techniques

author: David Nott
text: This paper explores the integration of Approximate Bayesian Computation ABC with Bayes Linear Analysis in the context of highdimensional statistical models As complex data structures and intricate probabilistic models continue to emerge traditional Bayesian methods may become infeasible due to computational demands Our proposed framework harnesses the strengths of ABC which allows for likelihoodfree inference alongside the articulated structure of Bayes Linear Analysis which provides a systematic approach for uncertainty quantification and prediction We present a novel methodology that adapts the ABC process to highdimensional parameter spaces through the implementation of lowrank approximations and strategic sampling techniques The resulting approach significantly mitigates computational burdens while maintaining accuracy in posterior estimates We illustrate the utility of our framework through simulations and applications to realworld datasets demonstrating improvements in efficiency and scalability over existing methodologies This work not only paves the way for more accessible Bayesian inference in highdimensional scenarios but also contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between different Bayesian paradigms

author: David Nott
text: The ensemble Kalman filter is the method of choice for many difficult highdimensional filtering problems in meteorology oceanography hydrology and other fields In this note we show that a common variant of the ensemble Kalman filter is an approximate Bayesian computation ABC algorithm This is of interest for a number of reasons First the ensemble Kalman filter is an example of an ABC algorithm that predates the development of ABC algorithms Second the ensemble Kalman filter is used for very highdimensional problems whereas ABC methods are normally applied only in very lowdimensional problems Third recent state of the art extensions of the ensemble Kalman filter can also be understood within the ABC framework

author: David Nott
text: The effects of different parametrizations on the convergence of Bayesian computational algorithms for hierarchical models are well explored Techniques such as centering noncentering and partial noncentering can be used to accelerate convergence in MCMC and EM algorithms but are still not well studied for variational Bayes VB methods As a fast deterministic approach to posterior approximation VB is attracting increasing interest due to its suitability for large highdimensional data Use of different parametrizations for VB has not only computational but also statistical implications as different parametrizations are associated with different factorized posterior approximations We examine the use of partially noncentered parametrizations in VB for generalized linear mixed models GLMMs Our paper makes four contributions First we show how to implement an algorithm called nonconjugate variational message passing for GLMMs Second we show that the partially noncentered parametrization can adapt to the quantity of information in the data and determine a parametrization close to optimal Third we show that partial noncentering can accelerate convergence and produce more accurate posterior approximations than centering or noncentering Finally we demonstrate how the variational lower bound produced as part of the computation can be useful for model selection

author: David Nott
text: The Laplace approximation is a foundational technique for approximating integrals of the form e dx in statistical inference and Bayesian analysis This paper presents a generalization of the classical Laplace approximation extending its applicability to a broader class of functions and multidimensional integrals We introduce a refined methodology that accommodates more complex landscapes of the function fx including those with multiple local minima and saddle points Through a combination of perturbation techniques and higherorder Taylor expansions we derive an asymptotic expansion that quantifies the corrections to the standard Laplace approximation Additionally we showcase our generalized approach through several empirical examples demonstrating improvements in accuracy and convergence rates in practical applications particularly in highdimensional parameter spaces The proposed framework not only enhances the robustness of the Laplace method but also provides a pathway for future research on approximation techniques in statistics Our findings suggest that this generalization can significantly aid in developing more efficient algorithms for inference in complex Bayesian models

author: David Nott
text: Laplace approximation is one commonly used approach to the calculation of difficult integrals arising in Bayesian inference and the analysis of random effects models Here we outline a procedure which is an extension of the Laplace approximation and which attempts to find changes of variable for which the integrand becomes approximately a product of onedimensional functions When the integrand is a product of onedimensional functions an approximation to the integral can be obtained using onediniensional quadrature The approximation is exact for a broader class of functions than the ordinary Laplace approximation and can be applied when the integrand is not smooth at lie mode As an illustration of this last point we consider Calculation of marginal likelihoods for smoothing parameter selection in the lasso C Elsevier BV

text: Dirichlet Process Mixture Models DPMMs are powerful tools for nonparametric clustering allowing for flexible modeling of data with an unknown number of clusters However traditional fitting methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC approaches often suffer from computational inefficiencies particularly in large datasets In this paper we propose a novel sequential algorithm that significantly enhances the speed and efficiency of fitting DPMMs Our method leverages sequential data processing and an adaptive sampling strategy to incrementally update cluster assignments and parameters facilitating realtime inference We provide a theoretical foundation for our algorithm proving its consistency and convergence properties Through extensive simulations and realworld applications we demonstrate that our sequential approach outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed and accuracy achieving comparable or superior clustering results in significantly shorter computational time This work highlights the potential of sequential algorithms in advancing the practical use of DPMMs and opens avenues for further exploration in nonparametric statistical methods

author: David Nott
text: Bayes linear analysis and approximate Bayesian computation ABC are techniques commonly used in the Bayesian analysis of complex models In this article we connect these ideas by demonstrating that regressionadjustment ABC algorithms produce samples for which firstand secondorder moment summaries approximate adjusted expectation and variance for a Bayes linear analysis This gives regressionadjustment methods a useful interpretation and role in exploratory analysis in highdimensional problems As a result we propose a new method for combining highdimensional regressionadjustment ABC with lowerdimensional approaches such as using Markov chain Monte Carlo for ABC This method first obtains a rough estimate of the joint posterior via regressionadjustment ABC and then estimates each univariate marginal posterior distribution separately in a lowerdimensional analysis The marginal distributions of the initial estimate are then modified to equal the separately estimated marginals thereby providing an improved estimate of the joint posterior We illustrate this method with several examples Supplementary materials for this article are available online

author: David Nott
text: In this article we propose an improvement on the sequential updating and greedy search SUGS algorithm for fast fitting of Dirichlet process mixture models The SUGS algorithm provides a means for very fast approximate Bayesian inference for mixture data which is particularly of use when datasets are so large that many standard Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithms cannot be applied efficiently or take a prohibitively long time to converge In particular these ideas are used to initially interrogate the data and to refine models such that one can potentially apply exact data analysis later on SUGS relies upon sequentially allocating data to clusters and proceeding with an update of the posterior on the subsequent allocations and parameters which assumes this allocation is correct Our modification softens this approach by providing a probability distribution over allocations with a similar computational cost this approach has an interpretation as a variational Bayes procedure and hence we term it variational SUGS VSUGS It is shown in simulated examples that VSUGS can outperform in terms of density estimation and classification a version of the SUGS algorithm in many scenarios In addition we present a data analysis for flow cytometry data and SNP data via a threeclass Dirichlet process mixture model illustrating the apparent improvement over the original SUGS algorithm
